items.title: Bacteria swap genes like trading cards
items.claim: Sexual reproduction is supposedly biology's great innovation for mixing genes. Bacteria don't bother. They share DNA fragments — including whole antibiotic-resistance genes — directly between unrelated species, sometimes across genera.

options.text: Useful mutations spread across the bacterial 'pan-genome' far faster than vertical inheritance allows — antibiotic resistance can jump from one species to another in a single transfer event
Bacteria only share genes within the same species
Horizontal transfer is too rare to matter

items.reveal_title: Three mechanisms keep the bacterial gene pool fluid
items.reveal:
Conjugation: two bacteria form a physical bridge (pilus) and transfer a plasmid.
Transformation: bacteria scoop up loose DNA from the environment.
Transduction: viruses (phages) accidentally package bacterial DNA and inject it into the next host.

The NDM-1 resistance gene, first found in Klebsiella in 2008, jumped via plasmids across at least 11 bacterial species and 4 continents within a decade. Genes encoding beta-lactamases (penicillin breakdown) appear in soil bacteria; clinical pathogens picked them up after antibiotics entered hospitals.

The 'tree of life' for bacteria isn't really a tree — it's a tangled net.
items.why: Evolution is taught as descent with modification along branching lineages. Bacterial evolution is reticular — sideways, not just downward.

items.title: Your body can make antibodies against molecules that don't exist yet
items.claim: Humans have about 20,000 genes. We make perhaps 10 to the 11 different antibody molecules — far more than our genome could encode directly. Including antibodies against viruses we'll never meet.
items.prompt: How do we generate such enormous antibody diversity?

options.text: Each antibody is encoded by a separate gene

V(D)J recombination — during B cell development, gene segments (V, D, J) are randomly chosen and joined with imprecise cuts, and then somatic hypermutation refines the result during an immune response
Antibodies are made up new for each encounter from scratch
The genome reshuffles itself constantly in all cells

items.reveal_title: Tonegawa's discovery — recombination in somatic cells
items.reveal:
Susumu Tonegawa (Nobel 1987) showed that B cells deliberately rearrange their immunoglobulin genes. Each B cell randomly picks one V, one D and one J segment for the heavy chain (V and J for the light chain), joins them with imprecise junctions (adding/deleting nucleotides), and pairs heavy with light. The combinatorial maths gives about 10 to the 11 possible specificities from a few hundred gene segments.

Once a B cell encounters its antigen, somatic hypermutation introduces additional point mutations into the variable region, and selection retains the best binders (affinity maturation).

The result is an immune system that can respond to virtually any molecular shape — including ones never seen before, like artificial drugs.
items.why: Genome size limits direct encoding. The immune system uses combinatorics and somatic mutation to overshoot what the genome alone could specify.

items.title: Plants tell the date by measuring the LENGTH of the night
items.claim: Chrysanthemums flower in autumn. Spinach bolts in long-day summer. Plants 'know' the time of year. They don't measure day length — they measure how long the night is, by counting protein degradation events.
items.prompt: What molecules let plants measure night length?

options.text: Phytochromes — light-absorbing pigments that switch between two forms (Pr and Pfr); the ratio shifts in the dark by slow Pfr decay, and the time taken to reach a threshold tells the plant how long the night was

items.reveal:
Phytochrome exists in two interconverting forms: Pr (red-absorbing) and Pfr (far-red-absorbing). Red light (660 nm) converts Pr to Pfr; far-red light (730 nm) reverses it. In darkness, Pfr slowly degrades back to Pr.

Day-length detection works on NIGHT length. Interrupting a long night with a brief flash of red light is enough to convert Pr to Pfr and 'reset' the plant — and shows that the plant is timing darkness, not light. Far-red light reverses the effect (Borthwick, Hendricks 1950s).

Short-day plants (chrysanthemums, soybeans, rice) flower when nights exceed a critical length. Long-day plants (spinach, wheat, lettuce) flower when nights are shorter than a critical length. Day-neutral plants (tomatoes, sunflowers) flower at a certain age.

The signal travels from leaves to apical meristem. The mobile signal — long sought as 'florigen' (Chailakhyan 1937) — was finally identified in 2007 as the FT protein (FLOWERING LOCUS T).

Agricultural exploitation: greenhouses can artificially adjust day length to force flowering year-round. Cut-flower industries rely on photoperiod manipulation.
items.why: Plants seem time-blind. They use a beautiful molecular clock built from light-reversible pigments — and they care about the dark, not the light.
